1135.title: Ninth commandment (CCC 2517–2533)
1135.hook: purity of heart lets us see God in others
1135.howItsDone: Catholics pray for purity of heart and examine their thoughts and looks before confession; the Church teaches chastity, modesty, purity of intention and prayer as helps in this struggle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth and beauty: real beauty can tell the truth. Your line was beauty is true.

A smudge on a pair of glasses. The wearer doesn't notice it at first. The world just seems a little gray, a little blurred at the edges, and faces look tired. Then the glasses come off, get a wipe on a shirt, go back on, and everything is sharp again. Nothing out there changed. The lens did. The ninth commandment, in the Catechism, turns out to be about lenses: what we look at people through.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON YOUR GLASSES.` → `NOTHING OUT THERE CHANGED.` → `THE LENS DID.`

segments.voice: As the Catechism counts them, the ninth commandment forbids coveting a neighbor's wife: disordered desire, which it calls concupiscence. But it builds the whole section on a line from the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." The heart here isn't just feelings. The Catechism calls it the seat of the moral personality; in plain words, where intentions are born. The pure of heart have tuned mind and will to God's ways, in charity, chastity, love of truth and faith. Then the promise opens in a surprising direction. Seeing God is the end of the road, but purity of heart lets us see according to God now: the other person as a neighbor, and the human body, ours and others', as a temple of the Holy Spirit. That's the smudge wiped off. Not a refusal to look at people, but a way of looking that doesn't reduce them. How does a heart get clean? The Catechism names a struggle and its helps: chastity, purity of intention, purity of vision, discipline over what feelings and imagination dwell on, and prayer. It adds modesty, which protects the private center of a person and refuses to unveil what should stay hidden. And it's grace as well as effort: no one cleans the lens entirely alone. The ninth commandment is less a list of things not to see than a promise about what you'll be able to see.
screen: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.` · `THE HEART: WHERE INTENTIONS ARE BORN.` · `SEE OTHERS AS GOD SEES THEM.` · `CHASTITY, INTENTION, VISION, PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three faces: someone you love, someone you pass every day without really seeing, and someone you find hard. One at a time, set down the label you usually put on them and look for the person underneath. If you pray, ask to see each one as God sees them; if not, simply let them be more than you thought.
Purity of heart. A heart tuned to God in love, chastity, truth and faith, which, in Catholic teaching, begins to see others, and God, clearly. Today's word.
Your line: they shall see god. A clean heart changes what the eyes can see. Until tomorrow.

1136.title: Tenth commandment (CCC 2534–2557)
1136.hook: envy and greed versus poverty of heart
1136.howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves for envy and greed before confession, and the Church teaches good will, humility, trust in providence and detachment from riches as the remedies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth commandment and purity of heart, the clean lens. Your line was they shall see god.

A friend posts the news: the job came through. The new house. The engagement ring, a close-up of the hand. And for some people there's a half-second, before typing congratulations, when something in the chest tightens. Not hatred. Nothing anyone would confess out loud. Just a small, sour question: why them? Stealing, lying, killing are things done. The last commandment, like the ninth, goes underneath the doing, to that half-second.
screen: `THE JOB CAME THROUGH.` → `A HALF-SECOND BEFORE CONGRATULATIONS.` → `WHY THEM?`

segments.voice: Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house." Wanting good things isn't the sin, the Catechism says; being hungry and wanting bread is fine. The commandment targets greed without limit, and the wish to get things unjustly, at a neighbor's cost. Then the quieter relative: envy, which the Catechism calls sadness at the sight of another's goods, and a wish to have them, even unjustly. The tight chest at the good news. It cites Augustine, who called envy the diabolical sin, and Pope Gregory the Great, who said that from envy come hatred, gossip, slander, and joy at a neighbor's misfortune. What does it offer instead? Good will, humility, and trust in God's providence. And it quotes John Chrysostom, who pictured rejoicing in a brother's progress as a way of giving glory to God. Then the heart of it. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The Catechism calls this poverty of heart: detachment from riches, so our hold on things doesn't crowd out God. Not pretending you have nothing; just not being owned by what you have. And underneath it all is the desire the tenth commandment points toward: the longing to see God. The sour half-second is a hunger aimed at the wrong table. That closes Part Three of the Catechism, how we live. Part Four is about how we pray.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT COVET.` · `ENVY: SADNESS AT ANOTHER'S GOOD.` · `REJOICE IN A BROTHER'S PROGRESS.` · `POVERTY OF HEART.`

Notice any tight spot without scolding yourself, then slowly try to want it for them. If you pray, thank God for their gift by name; if you don't, wish them more of it.

1137.title: What prayer is (CCC 2559–2565)
1137.howItsDone: Catholics pray in many ways, alone and together, aloud and in silence; the Catechism opens its teaching on prayer by calling it a gift from God, a covenant relationship and a communion with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenth commandment and the end of Part Three: envy, greed, and poverty of heart. Your line was enough.

A well in Samaria, outside a town, and a stranger sitting on its edge, tired from walking. A woman comes out with her jar, around the sixth hour, the Gospel says. And the stranger speaks first. Not with a sermon. With a request. "Give me to drink." At the start of its fourth part, on prayer, the Catechism goes to that well. Before it says anything about how to pray, it notices who asked first.
screen: `A WELL IN SAMARIA.` → `A WOMAN WITH A JAR.` → `GIVE ME TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: At the end of year one, you met prayer as a relationship. Here is the Catechism's fuller picture, in three words: gift, covenant, communion. First, gift. It quotes Thérèse of Lisieux: prayer is a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven, a cry of thanks and of love in trial as in joy. And John Damascene: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God. Then something humbling: we don't know how to pray as we ought, so humility is where prayer begins. Which brings it to the well. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells the woman, "If thou didst know the gift of God," she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water. The Catechism reads the scene this way: it is Jesus who is thirsty, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Then Augustine: God thirsts that we may thirst for him. Whether we know it or not, prayer is the meeting of two thirsts. Second, covenant. Prayer comes from the heart, the hidden center of a person, the place of decision and of truth, where we choose life or death. And it's a covenant because it's a relationship God started, binding him and us together in Christ. Third, communion: the living relationship of God's children with their Father, with his Son Jesus Christ, and with the Holy Spirit. Not a technique. A life with someone. Before a single instruction, then, the Catechism says: you're not the one who started this.
screen: `PRAYER IS A GIFT.` · `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `PRAYER IS A COVENANT.` · `PRAYER IS COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: Don't try to say anything yet; picture the well, the heat, the jar, and the stranger who asks first, and notice your own thirst today, for rest, for peace, for someone to listen. If you pray, simply turn toward God, the way Thérèse put it, a simple look; if you don't, stay with the thirst without fixing it.
What prayer is. In Catholic teaching, a gift, a covenant and a communion: the raising of mind and heart to God, who comes looking for us first. Today's word.
Your line: god thirsts that we thirst. The thirst came looking for you first. See you tomorrow.

1138.title: Old Testament prayer (CCC 2568–2589)
1138.hook: Abraham listens, Moses intercedes, David praises, Elijah waits
1138.howItsDone: The Church prays the psalms each day in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Old Testament readings are heard at Mass; the Catechism presents Abraham, Moses, David and Elijah as teachers of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what prayer is: gift, covenant, communion, and a stranger at a well asking for a drink. Your line was god thirsts that we thirst.

Four people, four different places. An old man hearing his name called, and answering: here I am. A leader on a mountain, arguing with God for people who have just let him down. A king with a harp, singing. A prophet in a cave, worn out, waiting for a voice that isn't in the wind or the fire. In the Catechism, these four are among the teachers of prayer before Christ.
screen: `AN OLD MAN: HERE I AM.` → `A LEADER ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `A KING WITH A HARP.` → `A PROPHET IN A CAVE.`

segments.voice: Abraham first; you watched him bargain for Sodom back in year two. The Catechism says his heart was in tune with God's will, and his prayer showed first in deeds: he went, as the Lord told him. When God calls, Abraham answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "Here I am." Listening as prayer. Readiness. And he dared to plead for Sodom: even the listener speaks up. Moses next. After the people made the golden calf, he stands between them and God and pleads for them. The Catechism calls this intercession, and notes that Moses doesn't pray for himself, but for the very people who made his life hard. Exodus says the Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to a friend; intercession grows out of friendship. Then David, the king after God's own heart, a shepherd who prays for his people and in their name. His prayer is praise and repentance, and tradition ties psalms to his name. Praise, in his hands, is music. Last, Elijah. On Mount Carmel he prays and fire comes down. Later he flees into the desert, exhausted, and on the mountain of God he waits. The Lord is not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire. Then comes what the Douay-Rheims calls "a whistling of a gentle air," and there Elijah meets the Lord. Waiting is prayer too. Listen, intercede, praise, wait: lessons learned slowly, a long school before the Gospels.
screen: `ABRAHAM: HERE I AM.` · `MOSES: PLEADING FOR OTHERS.` · `DAVID: PRAISE AS MUSIC.` · `ELIJAH: A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the four and take that posture: Abraham, simply ready, saying here I am if you pray; Moses, asking good for someone who has let you down; David, naming one thing that deserves praise; Elijah, doing nothing at all and waiting for the quiet underneath the noise. Stay with the one you chose, whether you pray it or simply try it on.
Old Testament prayer. In Catholic teaching, the long school of prayer before Christ: Abraham's readiness, Moses' pleading, David's praise, Elijah's waiting. Today's word.
Your line: the long school. Readiness, pleading, praise and waiting all count as prayer. That's today, done.

1139.title: Jesus prays (CCC 2598–2606)
1139.hook: he prays at every big moment of his life
1139.howItsDone: Catholics look to Jesus as the model of prayer, and some keep his habits: prayer before decisions, time alone in quiet, thanksgiving, and the garden's handing over of the will, echoed in the Lord's Prayer's thy will be done.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Old Testament prayer: Abraham listening, Moses pleading, David singing, Elijah waiting. Your line was the long school.

Before a big choice, out comes the list. Pros, cons. A call to a friend, a night to sleep on it, other people's opinions scrolled at midnight. Luke's Gospel tells about the night before Jesus chose the twelve apostles, the men who would carry on his work. He didn't make a list. He went up a mountain to pray, and in the Douay-Rheims, "he passed the whole night in the prayer of God." When day came, he chose twelve.
screen: `PROS, CONS, MIDNIGHT.` → `UP A MOUNTAIN TO PRAY.` → `THE WHOLE NIGHT IN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Luke's Gospel, the Catechism points out, keeps showing Jesus praying at the turning points. At his baptism in the Jordan, while he prays, the heavens open. Before choosing the Twelve, a whole night. Before Peter says who Jesus is, he has been praying alone. On the mountain of the Transfiguration, his face changes as he prays. And a quieter habit: he often slipped away to lonely places, sometimes at night, to pray. Where did he learn? As a boy, the Catechism says, Jesus learned to pray with his human heart from his mother, and in the synagogue and the Temple, with the words and rhythms of his people. Yet his prayer comes from somewhere deeper: his relationship with the Father. Listen to how his prayers begin. At the tomb of Lazarus, before he calls his friend out, he says, "Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me." Thanks, before the miracle. Then the garden, the night before he dies, in Luke: "not my will, but thine be done." The garden, the Catechism says, gives a glimpse of the depth of his prayer as Son: trust, and a will handed over. Mark keeps the Aramaic word he used: Abba, Father. Even on the cross he prays, for the ones crucifying him, and at the end he commends his spirit into his Father's hands. In the Catechism's picture, Jesus isn't only the one Christians pray to. He prayed first, and taught by doing it.

If you pray, bring it to God, and if you're ready, add the words from the garden. If you don't, let it rest in quiet before you decide.

1140.title: Mary prays (CCC 2617–2619)
1140.howItsDone: Catholics say Mary's fiat in the Angelus, where be it done unto me according to thy word is one of its lines, and the Magnificat is sung or said at Vespers, the evening prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus prays: a whole night before choosing the Twelve, thanks before the miracle, not my will but thine. Your line was he prayed first.

Two scenes, close together in Luke's Gospel. In the first, a woman in Nazareth hears an angel's message that will rearrange her whole life, and she answers in one sentence. In the second, she has walked into the hill country to see her cousin Elizabeth, and when Elizabeth greets her, she doesn't answer in one sentence. She sings. A short yes, and then a long song.
screen: `NAZARETH: ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE HILL COUNTRY: A SONG.` → `A SHORT YES, A LONG SONG.`

segments.voice: You've met both scenes before; today the Catechism reads them as prayer. The angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son. She asks how. He answers. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, that be it done is one word: fiat. The Catechism says simply: this is Christian prayer, to be wholly God's, because he is wholly ours. It isn't a request. It's an offering. She doesn't know what comes next, and she says yes anyway. Then the second prayer. Elizabeth calls her blessed, and Mary answers: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin it begins Magnificat, and that's the song's name. The Catechism calls it the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church. It sings that God has scattered the proud, put down the mighty, lifted up the lowly, and filled the hungry with good things. Praise, in Mary's mouth, is not polite. It's a song about the world turned right side up. One more moment: at a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus, then tells the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." The Catechism sees her there asking on behalf of others, and pointing them toward her Son. First yes, then praise, and all along, pointing past herself.
screen: `BE IT DONE TO ME: FIAT.` · `WHOLLY GOD'S.` · `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.`

segments.voice: First the yes: bring to mind one thing you've been resisting, something you can't control, and without solving it, try letting it be; if you pray, borrow Mary's words, be it done to me according to thy word. Then the praise: name, slowly, a few good things that are real today. If you don't pray, let yes and gladness simply sit side by side.
Mary prays. Her fiat at the Annunciation, be it done to me, and her Magnificat at the Visitation, my soul doth magnify the Lord: in Catholic teaching, yes to God, then praise. Today's word.
Your line: yes, then praise. Her yes came before she knew what came next. See you tomorrow.

1141.title: Five forms (CCC 2626–2643)
1141.howItsDone: The Mass holds the forms of prayer together: praise in the Gloria, petition and intercession in the prayers of the faithful, and thanksgiving in the Eucharistic Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary prays: her fiat, be it done to me, and her Magnificat. Your line was yes, then praise.

One kitchen, one ordinary day, two people who love each other. Good morning, glad you're here. Could you grab milk on the way home? Call your sister, she's having a hard week. Thank you for dinner. And once, out of nowhere: you're amazing, you know that? Greeting, asking, asking for someone else, thanks, and plain admiration. Nobody learns those as categories. They're just what love sounds like. The Catechism names the same shapes in prayer.
screen: `GOOD MORNING. COULD YOU GRAB MILK?` → `CALL YOUR SISTER.` → `THANK YOU. YOU'RE AMAZING.`

segments.voice: First, blessing and adoration. Blessing, the Catechism says, is a meeting of God and the person: God blesses, and the heart blesses back the source of every blessing. Adoration is the creature standing before the Creator, and knowing it. Second, petition: asking. Asking shows we know what we are: creatures, not our own beginning. And the first thing to ask for is forgiveness, then the kingdom, before anything else. Third, intercession: asking for someone else. This is what Jesus does for us, and Christian intercession has no boundaries; it reaches even enemies. Fourth, thanksgiving. Every event and every need can become an offering of thanks, and the Catechism quotes the line from Paul you met in year two, in the Douay-Rheims: "In all things give thanks." It ties thanksgiving to the Eucharist, whose Greek name means thanksgiving. Fifth, praise, and here the Catechism draws a fine line. Praise gives God glory for his own sake, beyond anything he does, simply because he is. Thanks answers a gift; praise, in that picture, asks for nothing. And the Eucharist gathers all of them into one. The week in one breath: they shall see God; enough; God thirsts that we thirst; the long school; he prayed first; yes, then praise; and now, five ways to speak.
screen: `BLESSING AND ADORATION.` · `PETITION, THEN INTERCESSION.` · `THANKSGIVING: IN ALL THINGS.` · `PRAISE: FOR WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Take each form for a few breaths, in your own words: blessing, noticing you stand before something larger than you; petition, one thing you need; intercession, one person who needs something; thanksgiving, one thing from today. Then praise: if you pray, say something to God that asks for nothing at all. If you don't pray, walk through the five as ways of paying attention.
Five forms. Blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise: in Catholic teaching, the shapes prayer takes, all gathered into the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: five ways to speak. Love already knows most of them by heart. That's the week.
